analysis.investment_thesis: NAPS Global fails the Magic Formula decisively: while the P/E of 5.91 implies a superficially attractive earnings yield (~17%), the ROE of 0.16% signals near-zero return on capital — this is a low-margin fabric-trading middleman, not a high-quality business. Cheap does not equal good, and the Magic Formula requires both.
key_strengths: Low P/E of 5.91 implies a high headline earnings yield (~17%)
key_risks: ROE of 0.16% indicates virtually no return on capital — fails the ROIC test
Commoditized fabric-trading business with no pricing power or moat
₹15.7 Cr micro-cap with low liquidity and limited disclosure
red_flags: ROE of 0.16% is essentially zero — earnings may be inflated by one-time items or working-capital accounting
Earnings quality suspect: a 5.91 P/E on 0.16% ROE is arithmetically odd (suggests very low equity base or one-off profit)
Pure trading businesses typically destroy capital over a cycle
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on two axes — how cheap (earnings yield) and how good (return on capital). NAPS Global appears cheap on the surface with a P/E of 5.91, translating to a ~17% earnings yield that would normally rank well. However, the second axis collapses the thesis: an ROE of 0.16% means the business generates essentially no return on the capital employed. Since ROIC is typically close to or below ROE for unlevered trading businesses, this is a textbook "cheap for a reason" setup. A fabric importer who buys and resells to garment makers has razor-thin margins, inventory/working-capital drag, and no structural moat — exactly the kind of business the Magic Formula is designed to screen out.

Systematically, I would not own this. The combination fails both the quantitative test (need ROIC >20%, getting ~0%) and the qualitative sanity check (trading middleman with no durable economics). The 70% promoter holding and tiny ₹15.7 Cr market cap also mean this is effectively a promoter-controlled microcap with limited float — not a setup where the Magic Formula's statistical edge reliably plays out. Skip it; there are thousands of Indian listed names and the formula only works when both criteria are satisfied.
